summary:
PROJECT ODYSSEY is an interactive 3D web game where the player becomes a space mission commander, designing, managing, and simulating a complete mission from concept to results.

It is built on real worlds with no fantasy: the Moon for training, then Mercury, Venus, Mars, Europa, and Titan. Each destination poses a different challenge, so a design that succeeds in one place can fail in another.

The journey runs through eight cinematic stages: choosing a destination, mission control, building the spacecraft and choosing a launch vehicle, launch, deep space, orbital insertion, discovery, and a final evaluation with multiple endings.

The player balances five counters: budget, mass, power, communications, and orbit. Every part added shows its effects immediately, and every decision has visible consequences.

Standout features:

Glowing threads that trace each decision’s impact.
A cinematic planet carousel.
A closing film built from the player’s own decisions.
A “What if?” button that tests the same design at another destination.

The game is bilingual (Arabic and English) with an instant toggle, and every term is explained simply so anyone can understand it. It is generated entirely in code to run fast and stay stable in front of a strict judging panel.

PROJECT ODYSSEY: Detailed Project Description

Overview

PROJECT ODYSSEY is an interactive 3D web game that puts the player in the role of a space mission commander. The player designs a spacecraft, chooses a rocket, manages limited resources, flies the mission, and finds out how every decision shaped the result. It answers the competition’s challenge directly: students rarely get to experience an entire mission, so the trade-offs stay abstract. Here they become something the player sees and feels.

The game uses only real destinations and real physical principles. There is no fantasy. Creativity comes from the presentation, the interaction design, and the way consequences are shown.

The Destinations

The player chooses from six real worlds, picked so that each one stresses a different part of the design:

  • Moon: the training level. It is close and forgiving, with a signal delay of about 1.3 seconds.
  • Mercury: abundant sunlight but extreme heat, and slowing down to enter orbit takes a great deal of fuel.
  • Venus: a crushing, burning atmosphere where a lander lasts only hours, so radar is the key instrument.
  • Mars: dust storms that weaken solar power, long signal delays, and weeks of blackout when the planet passes behind the Sun.
  • Europa: sunlight at roughly 4% of Earth’s level and radiation strong enough to destroy electronics.
  • Titan: extreme distance and cold, with sunlight around 1% of Earth’s, which makes nuclear power almost essential.

Because of these differences, the same spacecraft can succeed at one destination and fail at another.

The Eight-Stage Journey

  1. The Call: a cinematic opening and a planet carousel for choosing the destination and the mission type (exploration, search for life conditions, resource discovery, or scientific observation).
  2. Mission Control: the player ranks scientific objectives, picks an architecture (orbiter, lander, or probe), chooses a direct or gravity-assist trajectory, and sets the mission duration. Five holographic advisors comment on the plan.
  3. Build the Explorer: the player assembles a 3D spacecraft from power systems, antennas, instruments, propulsion, thermal protection, and navigation, then picks a launch vehicle that must be strong enough for the total weight.
  4. The Launch: a pre-launch checklist, a countdown, and a real-time cinematic launch of the player’s own design.
  5. Deep Space: a time-lapse cruise where events like solar storms, navigation drift, and power dips demand decisions.
  6. Orbital Insertion: the player plans an orbit by altitude, tilt, and shape, sees the effects on imaging, radiation, and communication, then executes the burn.
  7. The Discovery: the player schedules instruments and data transmission, and results appear as maps, graphs, and discoveries.
  8. Mission Complete: a short film built from the player’s decisions, six scores, one of several endings, and an explanation of why the mission ended that way.

The Core Mechanic: Five Counters

All nine elements in the brief (objectives, spacecraft design, instruments, launch vehicle, budget, power, mass, communications, orbital constraints) are folded into five easy-to-read counters: budget, mass, power, communications, and orbit/fuel. They are linked. A bigger instrument needs more power and weight, more weight needs a stronger and costlier rocket and more fuel, and a bigger antenna sends more data home but adds mass. A simulation engine calculates all of this, and every animation reflects its numbers rather than being decoration.

What Makes It Creative

  • Ripple Lines: glowing threads travel from a newly added part to every counter it affects.
  • Planet carousel: an elegant destination picker with a zoom-and-blur transition, inspired by the reference video.
  • Blueprint to solid: parts appear as holograms, then become real components.
  • Light-delay pulse: commands travel visibly to the spacecraft with the destination’s true signal delay.
  • What-If replay: the same design is tested at another destination to prove the trade-offs are real.
  • Decision film: the ending is assembled from what the player actually did.

Understandable by Anyone

Every technical term is explained in one plain sentence with an everyday analogy, in both Arabic and English, with an instant language toggle and full right-to-left support. The Moon tutorial guides newcomers, and nothing requires outside knowledge.

Technical Approach and Quality

The game runs in the browser using Three.js. The planets, spacecraft textures, and sound are generated in code, so it loads quickly and has no asset dependencies. The simulation is separate from the visuals and uses a seeded random generator, so the same seed and decisions always give the same result. Quality adjusts automatically to the device, with a Safe Mode and a fallback for devices without WebGL. A hidden judge panel shows a live requirements checklist and a readable cause-and-effect log.
